meta.one_idea: A list keeps many values under one name, in order. You reach each value by its position, positions start at 0, and a slice stops just before its stop number.
outcomes: Make a list with square brackets and commas, and say what print shows for it.
Use len and a position number to reach any item, and know that the last position is len minus 1.
Predict what +, += [x] and * do to a list.
Read a slice with a start, a stop and a step, and say which items it takes.
Tell an index that crashes (road_trip[6]) from a slice that does not (road_trip[4:10]).

build_contract: One self-contained HTML file. It opens offline from a USB stick and makes no network request.
It opens in presenter view. There is no sidebar, top bar or button the instructor has to use.

Right arrow or the clicker is one press. Left arrow goes back one press. F goes full screen, A shows all the cards, and End shows the whole card at once. The instructor guide tells the instructor these keys, so they must work.
Every card is its own screen, in the order of this spec. Press 1 is what shows when the card opens.
Every card's outer element carries data-spec="<card id>" and data-presses="<number of presses>". The review script reads both.
No link to any other file. The students' handout and the instructor guide are separate files, and a link from this file is how a class finds the answers.
rules: No autoplay. Nothing moves on a timer. One press, one move, with a caption that says what just happened.
Commit, then reveal. Where a card asks a question, the answer shows only on the press after the room has answered.
Wrong answers stay private. No names, no per-student results on screen. Hands are counted out loud, never shown.
The topic is named once. Nothing before the title card says today's topic, not a heading, not a caption, not a file name on a code card.

Words are exact. Words in quotation marks, and every line under Exact words, are final. The rest of a press describes what happens, in your own design. If an exact line does not fit, ask for a new one; do not rewrite it.
Code is exact. Copy code and outputs from the JSON, never retype them. Every output here came from running the program.
Simple English. Short sentences, everyday words. No em-dashes anywhere, the page title included.
Every card moves. A card that introduces an idea steps; a static card is a picture of a lecture.

list_b = ["a", "b", "c"]
list_c = list_a + list_b

cards.purpose: Use slices and a loop to add up part of a list, inside a real problem.
cards.heading: Ravi's canteen week
show: Ravi wrote down what he spent at the canteen each day this week, Monday to Sunday.
Print how much he spent on weekdays (Monday to Friday), then on the weekend.
Use a slice for each part and a loop to add it up.
Type both totals on your worksheet.

presses.screen: The story, the list with Mon to Sun under its boxes, the steps, the output format with the totals as dots, and a 5 minute timer.
presses.say: Say the hint once: which positions are Monday to Friday? Start the timer.
presses.room: Code in the playground, type totals on the worksheet.

presses.screen: One worked solution, written in, and its output.
presses.say: Show it only after the timer. Point at spend[0:5] and spend[5:7].

must: The totals are not on screen until the second press.
must_not: Mention sum(). It has not been taught; a loop is the tool here.

data.solution:
spend = [60, 45, 80, 30, 55, 140, 110]
weekdays = 0
for amount in spend[0:5]:
    weekdays += amount
weekend = 0
for amount in spend[5:7]:
    weekend += amount
print("Weekdays:", weekdays)
print("Weekend:", weekend)
